By 1577 a small Plymouth ship called the Pelican slipped out of Plymouth Sound at the head of five ships, carrying Francis Drake, about 164 men and a secret commission from Elizabeth herself. Three years later Drake returned to Plymouth in his renamed flagship Golden Hind, having sailed around the entire world — only the second captain in history to do so. While Drake counted his Spanish silver, a separate set of voyages was probing the coast of North America, and by 1585 Sir Walter Raleigh had landed the first English settlers on Roanoke Island in modern-day North Carolina. Drake’s circumnavigation and the failed Virginia colony are two halves of the same Elizabethan ambition — reach further, trade more, beat Spain — but they ended very differently.

Key Fact

Elizabethan exploration was driven by the desire to expand trade beyond cloth markets in northern Europe, the chance to attack Spanish shipping for gold and silver, the search for a north-west passage to Asia, and the patriotic and religious wish to challenge Catholic Spain. New ship designs (galleons), better navigation tools (astrolabe, quadrant, more accurate maps) and the printed sailing directions of Richard Hakluyt made longer voyages possible.

Why Did Elizabethans Sail Further?

English trade in 1558 was overwhelmingly with Antwerp — raw wool and finished cloth across the narrow seas. When religious wars in the Netherlands disrupted the Antwerp market in the 1560s, English merchants needed new outlets. Joint-stock trading companies were chartered to push into the Baltic, the Mediterranean, Russia and West Africa.

Three other motives mattered. First, Spain’s American empire flooded Europe with silver bullion every year — Elizabethan privateers wanted a share. Second, men like Sir Humphrey Gilbert and John Davis searched for a north-west passage through the Arctic to the riches of Asia, hoping to bypass Spanish and Portuguese routes. Third, the geographer Richard Hakluyt argued in his 1582 Divers Voyages Touching the Discoverie of America that England needed colonies for trade, prestige and as bases against Spain. Patriotic, Protestant and commercial arguments reinforced one another.

Ships, Maps and Sailors

The technology made it possible. The English galleon — refined under naval administrator Sir John Hawkins — had a longer, lower hull than the older Spanish carrack. It carried more cannon along its sides and could turn faster, ideal for the running gun battles that suited English captains. Astrolabes and quadrants let navigators measure latitude from the sun and the pole star; new printed charts (notably Mercator’s 1569 projection) made plotting long ocean courses easier. Logbooks recording wind patterns built up reliable knowledge of the Atlantic. By the 1580s an English captain could plan a voyage to West Africa, the Caribbean or even through the Strait of Magellan with a confidence unimaginable a generation earlier.

It is tempting to see Drake as a swashbuckling hero, knighted on his own deck. The same generation, however, included Sir John Hawkins, who from the 1560s ran Crown-backed voyages to West Africa where he attacked Portuguese ships and trafficked enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to sell to Spanish colonists in the Caribbean — voyages on which Drake sailed as a young man. The Edexcel spec foregrounds Drake’s circumnavigation, not Hawkins’s slaving raids, but a top-band answer is aware that English ‘exploration’ included violence and the trade in enslaved people, not only navigation. This course writes ‘enslaved person’, not ‘slave’.

Drake’s Circumnavigation, 1577–80

In December 1577 Drake left Plymouth with five ships, officially bound for the Mediterranean. The real plan, agreed in secret with Elizabeth, was to sail through the Strait of Magellan and raid Spanish silver shipping along the unprotected Pacific coast of South America. Of the original five ships, only the renamed Golden Hind reached the Pacific. Drake captured the Spanish treasure ship Nuestra Señora de la Concepción — nicknamed by sailors the Cacafuego — off the coast of Peru in March 1579, taking 26 tons of silver, 80 pounds of gold and chests of jewels. Rather than return through the Magellan Strait where the Spanish would be waiting, he sailed up the Pacific coast as far as modern-day California, claimed it for Elizabeth, and then crossed the Pacific to the Spice Islands and home around the Cape of Good Hope.

He reached Plymouth on 26 September 1580. The voyage’s plunder paid every investor a return of about £47 for every £1 invested — including Elizabeth, secretly the largest backer. The queen knighted Drake on the deck of the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581, an act of public defiance towards Philip II that horrified the Spanish ambassador.

Why Was the Circumnavigation Significant?

The voyage mattered for several reasons. Politically, it was a deliberate humiliation of Spain and the most provocative act of Elizabethan privateering yet. Economically, the bullion strengthened the Crown’s finances and turned circumnavigation from theory into a profitable speculation. Strategically, Drake had charted Pacific coasts the Spanish had assumed were closed to outsiders and proved that English ships and seamanship could match Spain’s. Personally, it confirmed Drake’s status as a national hero and Elizabeth’s most trusted privateer — the man she would send to ‘singe the King of Spain’s beard’ at Cadiz in 1587 and command against the Armada in 1588.

Key Fact

Drake left Plymouth in December 1577 and returned on 26 September 1580 in the Golden Hind, having captured the Spanish treasure ship Cacafuego off Peru. Investors received about £47 for every £1 invested. Elizabeth knighted Drake on the deck of the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581 — a deliberate insult to Philip II.

Raleigh and the Attempted Colonisation of Virginia

In 1584 Elizabeth granted Sir Walter Raleigh a six-year charter to colonise unclaimed land in North America. Raleigh, a court favourite, never sailed himself but financed the expeditions and named the new region Virginia in honour of the ‘Virgin Queen’. A scouting voyage in 1584 reached the Outer Banks of present-day North Carolina, where the captains met the Algonquian-speaking Indigenous peoples of Roanoke Island and brought back two men, Manteo and Wanchese, to London.

In April 1585 Raleigh dispatched Sir Richard Grenville with seven ships and about 600 men. Around 100 of them were left on Roanoke Island in August as the settlement. The first settlement was led by Ralph Lane, a soldier rather than a farmer, and consisted largely of soldiers and gentlemen rather than experienced cultivators or craftsmen. By summer 1586 they were starving, on poor terms with Wingina’s Roanoke people, and a passing English fleet under Drake (returning from raids in the Caribbean) took them home.

Why Did the First Settlement Fail?

Several causes combined. The colonists were unsuited to the work — soldiers and gentlemen, not farmers; food ran out within months. Relations with the Indigenous Roanoke people, fragile from the start, broke down after Lane killed Wingina in 1586, ending any hope of trade for food. Roanoke Island itself had a poor harbour for resupply ships. The promised relief fleet from England was diverted to fight the Spanish in the Caribbean. And by 1587, Raleigh’s second attempt — led by John White and including women and children — arrived to find the first colony abandoned. White returned to England for supplies, was delayed by the Armada in 1588, and when he finally got back in 1590 the second settlement had vanished, leaving only the carved word CROATOAN. The fate of the ‘Lost Colony’ remains unknown.

The 16-mark essay reward is for weighing several causes — not for picking one. Top-band answers connect the failure of the first settlement (1585–86) and the disappearance of the second (1587–90) into a chain. The poor choice of colonists and a chosen leader (Lane) suited to soldiering rather than farming created food shortages; the killing of Wingina destroyed Indigenous co-operation; the Armada in 1588 prevented relief reaching the second colony just as it most needed it. Add Spain — the wider war pulled English shipping away from Roanoke at the critical moment — and you have a multi-cause judgement that an examiner can reward.

By 1588 Drake’s circumnavigation had given Elizabethan England a confident maritime self-image; Raleigh’s Roanoke had shown that ambition was not enough on its own. Both stories belong on the same page: an Age of Exploration that expanded trade and prestige, but did so unevenly, violently, and at a cost that the ‘Golden Age’ label hides.

In May 1588 the Spanish Armada sailed from Lisbon: 130 ships and around 30,000 sailors and soldiers, under the reluctant command of the Duke of Medina Sidonia. Philip II had ordered the largest amphibious invasion ever attempted in northern Europe. By September the surviving fleet was being scattered by storms north of Scotland, and roughly half of it would never reach Spain. A strong answer explains why — weighing English ships, Spanish supply, leadership, the fireships at Calais and the storms together, not picking one factor.

Key Fact

The Armada failed for four interconnected reasons: English ship design and gunnery (longer-range guns and faster ‘race-built’ galleons designed by Hawkins), the failure of the ‘join with Parma’ plan, English fireships at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588, and the storms that scattered the fleet around Scotland and Ireland in September.

Spanish Invasion Plans

Philip II’s plan rested on a difficult piece of geography. The Armada would sail from Lisbon up the Channel to Calais. There it would meet the Duke of Parma’s 30,000 veteran troops in the Spanish Netherlands, escort them across the Channel in unprotected barges, and land in Kent. Once Parma’s army was on English soil, Catholic English subjects would (Philip hoped) rise up. The fleet was therefore not just a war fleet but a transport bodyguard.

Two structural problems hurt the plan from the start. First, the ‘original’ commander Santa Cruz — an experienced admiral — died in February 1588. Philip replaced him with the Duke of Medina Sidonia, a senior nobleman who frankly admitted in writing that he had no naval experience. Second, the rendezvous with Parma assumed perfect timing: the Armada had to arrive off Calais exactly when Parma’s barges were ready. There was no deep-water port on the Flemish coast where the great Spanish galleons could shelter while they waited.

The English Fleet

The Lord High Admiral, Lord Howard of Effingham, commanded around 200 English ships from Plymouth. Drake was vice-admiral; Hawkins and Frobisher led other squadrons. Sir John Hawkins had spent the 1570s and 1580s redesigning English warships into race-built galleons — lower hulls, no high ‘castles’ at bow and stern, and a long line of long-range guns down each side. The Spanish fleet, by contrast, was designed to grapple-and-board: bigger, taller, packed with soldiers, but slower and with shorter-range cannon mounted differently.

The English knew they could not stop the Armada by ramming or boarding. Their plan was to use longer-range gunfire to keep the fight at a distance, harass the formation, and use the wind to attack from the rear — never letting Spain force a close-quarters fight on Spanish terms.

The Channel Battles, 31 July – 6 August

The Armada was first sighted off the Lizard on 19 July. From 31 July to 6 August the two fleets fought a running battle up the English Channel: skirmishes off Plymouth (31 July), Portland Bill (2 August) and the Isle of Wight (3–4 August). The Spanish kept their disciplined crescent formation; the English snapped at the wings, picked off a few stragglers (most notably the Rosario, captured by Drake), but never broke the Spanish line. By 6 August the Armada was anchored off Calais, waiting for word from Parma.

The Fireships at Calais, Night of 7–8 August

Parma’s news was bad: his barges were not ready, and the Dutch ‘Sea Beggars’ were blockading the inshore waters around Dunkirk. The Armada could not approach to take Parma’s troops on board; Parma could not come out. Lord Howard chose his moment. On the night of 7–8 August he sent eight unmanned fireships, packed with pitch and gunpowder and set on fire, drifting on the tide into the anchored Spanish fleet.

The fireships caused little physical damage — the Spanish cut their anchor cables and scattered — but the loss of formation was disastrous. Anchors were left on the seabed off Calais. The crescent never reformed.

The Battle of Gravelines, 8 August

The next day the English caught the broken Armada off Gravelines and fought the only sustained pitched battle of the campaign. Closing to within musket range, the English used their long-range guns to hammer the Spanish hulls for eight hours. Three Spanish galleons were sunk or driven aground; many others were badly damaged. The Spanish formation was wrecked, and the wind swung to the south-west, pushing the Armada into the North Sea, away from Parma, and away from any chance of return.

The Long Way Home

Medina Sidonia took the only route left: north around Scotland and west of Ireland to reach Spain. In September violent Atlantic storms scattered the fleet. The unseasoned water casks — a direct legacy of Drake’s 1587 raid on Cadiz — leaked, leaving crews dehydrated. Around two dozen ships were wrecked on the Scottish and Irish coasts; thousands of sailors and soldiers drowned or were killed by Crown soldiers when they crawled ashore. Of 130 ships that left Lisbon, fewer than 70 made it home, and most of those were unfit for further service.

Key Fact

On the night of 7–8 August 1588, Lord Howard sent eight English fireships into the anchored Spanish fleet at Calais. The fireships destroyed almost nothing but broke the Armada’s formation, prevented the planned link-up with Parma, and exposed the fleet to the English broadsides at Gravelines the next day.

Why the English Won — Weighing the Factors

A weak answer says ‘the weather beat the Armada’. Storms certainly destroyed the fleet on the way home, but by then the campaign was already lost — the storms killed a defeated Armada, not a winning one. The deeper causes interconnect.

‘The weather beat the Armada’ is a single-factor answer, and a judgement question needs several factors weighed. The storms hit AFTER the campaign was already decided. By 9 August the Armada had lost its formation at Calais, been mauled at Gravelines, missed Parma, and been blown into the North Sea. Top-band answers explain that the storms were the killing blow on a fleet that English ship design, English fireships, Spanish supply failures and the broken Parma plan had already defeated. Storms are part of the answer, not the answer.

English advantages came from preparation. Hawkins’s race-built galleons gave the fleet superior speed and gunnery. Drake’s Cadiz raid the previous April had destroyed the seasoned timber for water casks, leaving the Armada with leaking supplies. Lord Howard chose his moments well — the fireships at Calais were the single most important tactical decision of the campaign. Spanish problems were structural: Medina Sidonia’s inexperience, the missing deep-water port for the Parma rendezvous, the impossible coordination required between Lisbon and the Netherlands, and the Dutch Sea Beggars blockading the Flemish coast. The storms then finished the work the campaign had already begun.

For 16-mark judgement questions, weigh the factors and reach a defended overall view. A simple structure: short-term tactical reason (fireships and Gravelines), structural English advantages (Hawkins’s race-built ships and gunnery), Spanish failures (Medina Sidonia, no port, Parma plan), then the storms as finishing factor. Conclude on which mattered most and why — many strong answers argue the fireships were the decisive moment because they broke the formation that everything else depended on.

In 1558 Philip II of Spain had been Elizabeth’s brother-in-law, briefly proposed marriage, and was the dominant Catholic monarch of Europe. By 1587 his fleet was assembling at Lisbon to invade England. The drift from awkward alliance to open war took thirty years and pulled in religion, money, the Atlantic, and a small group of English seafarers who treated Spanish ships as legitimate prizes. By 1587 two decisive moves — English involvement in the Netherlands and Drake’s raid on Cadiz — had made war unavoidable.

Key Fact

Anglo-Spanish relations broke down across four strands: political (Mary’s execution and rival claims to the throne), religious (Protestant England versus Catholic Spain after 1570), commercial (privateering and clashes in the Atlantic), and military (English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 and Drake’s raid on Cadiz in 1587).

Political and Religious Rivalry

Through the 1560s the breakdown was slow. Philip II initially valued England as a buffer against France and tolerated Elizabeth’s Protestantism. The 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis changed the diplomatic weather: Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved Catholics of allegiance, recasting any Catholic monarch’s duty as removing her. The Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586) plots all featured Spanish backing or Spanish ambassadors. Mary, Queen of Scots was Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative ruler — her execution in February 1587 removed Philip’s diplomatic restraint.

Religion ran underneath all of this. Philip saw himself as the defender of the Catholic faith; the Counter-Reformation made the survival of Protestant England a personal affront. Recusancy fines, the execution of Catholic priests under the 1585 Act, and English support for the Dutch Protestant rebels all looked, from Madrid, like a Protestant crusade against Catholic Europe.

Commercial Rivalry — Privateering and Drake

Spain claimed a monopoly on trade with its American colonies under the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. English merchants disagreed. From the 1560s, captains such as John Hawkins (with Crown investment) ran trading voyages into the Spanish Caribbean, and from the early 1570s privateering exploded.

Sir Francis Drake was the most successful and most provocative privateer. In 1572–73 he raided Spanish silver convoys at Nombre de Dios in Panama. Between 1577 and 1580 he circumnavigated the globe in the Golden Hind, plundering Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America and returning with around £400,000 of treasure — roughly the value of a year’s Crown revenue. Elizabeth knighted him on his own ship at Deptford in 1581. Philip II read the knighthood as a deliberate insult: the queen of England was endorsing piracy.

Drake is often presented as an unambiguous English hero. The Edexcel B4 spec foregrounds his circumnavigation and his role against the Armada, and you should know those events well. But context matters: Drake had earlier sailed with John Hawkins on Crown-backed voyages that trafficked enslaved Africans to the Spanish Caribbean. The same decades that saw English ‘heroes’ tweak Spanish noses in the Atlantic were also building the early infrastructure of the transatlantic slave trade. Top-band judgement answers can know the spec content without absorbing the ‘Sea Dog’ legend uncritically.

English Involvement in the Netherlands

The Netherlands had been Spanish territory since 1556. Protestant unrest in the Netherlands from 1566 led Philip to send his most ruthless commander, the Duke of Alva, with 10,000 men in 1567; open war followed from 1568. Elizabeth had three reasons to worry. A Catholic Spanish-controlled Netherlands sat just across the Channel from Kent. Spanish armies in the Netherlands could ferry to England. And the suppression of Protestantism on her doorstep made her own position weaker.

Through the 1570s Elizabeth offered the Dutch covert support — money, English volunteers, harbour for Dutch ships — without committing troops officially. By 1584–85 the Dutch position was collapsing: William the Silent had been assassinated in July 1584, the Duke of Parma was steadily reconquering Dutch towns, and Antwerp fell in August 1585. In August 1585 Elizabeth signed the Treaty of Nonsuch, agreeing to send 7,400 men under Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, in support of the Dutch.

Leicester’s Expedition, 1585–87

Leicester’s expedition was a strategic and personal embarrassment. He fell out with the Dutch, accepted the title of Governor-General without Elizabeth’s permission (which the queen publicly repudiated), and lost the strategically important towns of Sluys and Deventer — the latter handed to Spain by an English Catholic deserter. His one famous engagement, Zutphen in September 1586, was a small skirmish best remembered for the death of the poet Sir Philip Sidney. Leicester returned home in disgrace in late 1587. The expedition failed militarily but succeeded diplomatically — Philip II treated the Treaty of Nonsuch as a formal declaration of war.

Drake’s Raid on Cadiz, 1587

By the spring of 1587 Philip’s invasion fleet was being assembled at Cadiz, Lisbon and the smaller Iberian ports. Elizabeth authorised Drake to disrupt it. On 19 April 1587 Drake led 23 ships into the harbour of Cadiz, fought past the Spanish defending galleys, and over the next two days destroyed around 30 Spanish warships and supply vessels — including barrels of seasoned wood needed for water casks. He then cruised the Iberian coast for weeks, attacking shipping and the fortress at Sagres.

Drake himself called it ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’. The raid did not destroy the Armada — it delayed it by about a year. The destruction of barrel-stave timber proved more important than the ships sunk: when the Armada finally sailed in July 1588, its water and provisions were stored in newer, unseasoned casks that leaked and spoiled at sea.

Key Fact

On 19 April 1587 Drake raided Cadiz with 23 ships, destroying around 30 Spanish vessels and barrels of seasoned wood for water casks. The raid delayed the Spanish Armada by roughly a year and contributed to its supply problems in 1588.

A middle-band answer lists privateering, religion, the Netherlands and Cadiz as separate causes. A top-band answer connects them: the 1570 papal bull (religion) made Catholic plots (Ridolfi, Babington) targeted at Mary politically explosive, which in turn drove Mary’s execution; meanwhile English privateering (Drake) had wrecked the commercial relationship and Crown finances; English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 were the strategic affront; Cadiz in 1587 was the open military challenge. By the time the Armada sailed, all four strands had hardened into a single Spanish decision to invade.

By the end of 1587 every restraining factor was gone. Mary was dead so Philip had a free hand. The Treaty of Nonsuch had committed England to the Dutch revolt. Drake had humiliated Spain at Cadiz. The papal bull was nearly two decades old. The Armada that left Lisbon in May 1588 was the product of all four strands — political, religious, commercial and military — not a sudden Spanish overreaction.

After the Northern Earls failed in open battle, Catholic resistance went underground. Between 1571 and 1586 three serious conspiracies aimed to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, Queen of Scots, and put her on the English throne with Spanish or French troops behind her. Each one was caught. The reason they were caught matters as much as the plots themselves: Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth’s Principal Secretary, had built the most sophisticated intelligence network in Europe.

Key Fact

The three major plots all centred on Mary, Queen of Scots: the Ridolfi Plot (1571) was a Spanish-backed plan to depose Elizabeth and crown Mary; the Throckmorton Plot (1583) was a French- and Spanish-backed invasion plan; the Babington Plot (1586) aimed to assassinate Elizabeth and was the trap that finally caught Mary.

The Ridolfi Plot, 1571

Roberto Ridolfi was a Florentine banker living in London with contacts in Madrid and Rome. His 1571 plan was to coordinate a Spanish invasion from the Netherlands under the Duke of Alva, an English Catholic rising led by the Duke of Norfolk, and the assassination of Elizabeth — all to put Mary on the throne and marry her to Norfolk.

Walsingham, then ambassador to France, intercepted coded correspondence and worked with Cecil to crack the cipher. Ridolfi himself was abroad when his courier was arrested at Dover with incriminating papers. Norfolk — already pardoned once for his role in 1569 — was arrested, tried for treason and executed in June 1572. Mary remained alive in custody, but Parliament now demanded harsher action against her.

The Throckmorton Plot, 1583

Francis Throckmorton was a young Catholic gentleman who acted as a courier between Mary and the Spanish ambassador in London, Bernardino de Mendoza. The 1583 plan was an invasion by French Catholic forces under the Duke of Guise, funded by Philip II of Spain, accompanied by an English Catholic rising. Walsingham’s agents had been watching Throckmorton for six months.

When his house was searched, agents found a list of English Catholic supporters and details of suitable invasion ports. Under torture, Throckmorton confessed; he was executed in July 1584. Mendoza was expelled from England — the last Spanish ambassador permitted on English soil. Parliament passed the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety, declaring that anyone in whose name a plot was made could be tried and executed. Mary was now legally exposed.

It is easy to picture Mary as the mastermind because every plot was named ‘for Mary’. In reality she was a closely watched prisoner moved between Tutbury, Sheffield, Chartley and Fotheringhay. Ridolfi was the Florentine banker’s scheme; Throckmorton was a courier passing letters; only the Babington Plot produced a letter in Mary’s own hand explicitly approving Elizabeth’s assassination — and even that exists because Walsingham deliberately allowed the correspondence to flow so that she would commit herself in writing. Top-band answers separate Mary’s claim (the magnet) from her active leadership (much smaller than the legend).

Walsingham’s Intelligence Network

By the early 1580s Sir Francis Walsingham — Principal Secretary from 1573 — ran an intelligence service of around 50 agents across England and Europe, paid for partly out of his own pocket. His chief cryptanalyst, Thomas Phelippes, could break almost any contemporary cipher. Agents intercepted letters, opened them, copied them, recoded them and sent them on so the recipients suspected nothing. Catholic priests entering England were tracked from the moment they landed. Imprisoned suspects were interrogated, often under torture authorised by the Privy Council.

For the Mary problem specifically, Walsingham organised what would now be called a sting. He arranged for Mary to be moved to Chartley Hall in 1585 and let her believe she had a secret channel for letters — smuggled in beer barrels by a brewer. Every letter was already being read. The trap was set; he simply needed someone reckless enough to step into it.

The Babington Plot, 1586

Anthony Babington was a wealthy Catholic gentleman in his mid-twenties. In July 1586 he wrote to Mary outlining a plan to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, and welcome a Spanish-backed invasion. Walsingham’s team intercepted the letter, read it, copied it — and waited.

Mary’s reply on 17 July 1586 explicitly approved the assassination of Elizabeth. Phelippes added a forged postscript asking Babington to name his fellow conspirators, then resealed the letter and let it through. Babington named them. By August every plotter was in custody. Babington and six others were hanged, drawn and quartered in September 1586. Mary was tried at Fotheringhay Castle in October under the 1585 Act; her own letter sealed her fate.

Key Fact

Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October 1586 and condemned to death. Elizabeth delayed signing the warrant for months. When she finally signed in February 1587, William Cecil and the Privy Council acted immediately — Mary was beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587. Elizabeth publicly blamed her secretary, Davison, for sending the warrant.

Why Mary Was Executed in 1587

The execution had multiple causes. The Babington letter gave incontrovertible written proof, removing Elizabeth’s usual legal cover. The 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety had been designed for exactly this. Parliament and the Privy Council, especially William Cecil and Walsingham, had been pushing for years. Spanish preparations for an invasion fleet were already visible — killing Mary removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative monarch and put Spain in a corner. Elizabeth’s own famous prevarication — she signed, then claimed she had not meant the warrant to be used — reflected the political risk: executing an anointed queen was unprecedented and gave Philip II a Catholic martyr to exploit.

Connect the plots into a chain rather than describing each in turn. Ridolfi (1571) cost Norfolk his head and pushed Parliament to demand action against Mary. Throckmorton (1583) produced the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety. Babington (1586) gave the legal proof to use that Act against Mary herself. Each plot drove a tougher law that made the next plot easier to prosecute — and Mary’s execution in 1587 then removed Spain’s legitimate cover, leading directly to the Armada the following year.

The plots show two things. First, that the threat to Elizabeth was genuine and persistent — without Walsingham, Cecil, Phelippes and the network they ran, one of these schemes would probably have succeeded. Second, that Elizabeth was not making these decisions alone. Do not treat the Privy Council as a vague entity; the named figures — Cecil at Treasury, Walsingham at intelligence, Phelippes on ciphers — are the difference between a vague answer and a top-band one.

In November 1569, two of the most powerful Catholic nobles in England raised their tenants and marched south. Thomas Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and Charles Neville, Earl of Westmorland, restored the Catholic Mass at Durham Cathedral and headed for Tutbury, where Mary, Queen of Scots was being held. Their plan was to free Mary, marry her to the Duke of Norfolk, and force Elizabeth to name her Catholic heir. Within weeks the rising had collapsed without a single battle — but the panic in London was real, and the response shaped Elizabethan politics for the next twenty years.

Key Fact

The Revolt of the Northern Earls (November 1569 — January 1570) was led by the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland. Their aim was to free Mary, Queen of Scots from Tutbury, marry her to the Duke of Norfolk, and restore Catholicism in England.

Why the Earls Rebelled

The causes of the revolt stack on top of each other and need to be weighed, not just listed. The Earls had lost wealth, status and religious freedom under Elizabeth, and Mary’s presence in England from May 1568 made action feel possible at last.

Loss of noble power sat at the centre. Elizabeth had taken Crown lands back from northern lords, promoted ‘new men’ like William Cecil from the gentry, and reduced the role of the old Catholic Council of the North. Religion gave the grievance a banner. The 1559 settlement made Catholic worship illegal, and the Earls’ tenants were still loyal to the old faith. Mary’s arrival in England in 1568 then handed them a Catholic alternative on English soil. Finally, a court plot to marry Mary to the Duke of Norfolk, England’s only duke, suggested powerful southern Protestants might tolerate a Catholic succession too — until Elizabeth heard of it and arrested Norfolk in October 1569.

Students often write ‘the Northern Earls rebelled because they were Catholic’ and stop there. Top-band Edexcel answers separate the threads. Religion mattered — restoring the Mass at Durham was symbolic and the Pope would soon back them with the 1570 bull. But Northumberland had also lost a copper mine to the Crown and Westmorland had crippling debts; both had been pushed off the Council of the North. The revolt is causation: religious grievance + lost noble power + Mary’s arrival + the Norfolk marriage scheme, with each factor feeding the next.

What Happened, November 1569 — January 1570

On 9 November 1569 the Earls were summoned to court to explain themselves. Fearing a trap, they raised their tenants instead. By mid-November around 4,600 men had mustered at Brancepeth. On 14 November they entered Durham Cathedral, tore up the English Bible and prayer book, and held a Catholic Mass for the first time in a decade. They marched south as far as Bramham Moor, but never reached Tutbury — Elizabeth had already moved Mary to Coventry, well out of reach.

The Earl of Sussex, lord president of the Council of the North, raised a royal army of 14,000 men. The rebels, hopelessly outnumbered and finding little new support, melted away in December. Northumberland fled to Scotland; Westmorland escaped to the Spanish Netherlands. A second flicker of rebellion under Leonard Dacre in February 1570 was crushed at the Battle of Gelt Bridge.

Elizabeth’s Response

The retribution was deliberately savage. Elizabeth ordered around 450 rebels to be executed, mostly poorer tenants chosen by lottery so that every northern village saw a hanging. Lands belonging to the rebel leaders were seized, breaking the wealth of the Percy and Neville families for good. The Council of the North was reorganised under loyal Protestant control, ending the Earls’ old regional dominance. Northumberland was eventually handed back by the Scots and beheaded at York in 1572.

Key Fact

Even though it failed, the revolt mattered: it triggered the 1570 papal bull excommunicating Elizabeth, the 1571 Treasons Act making it illegal to deny Elizabeth was queen, harsher recusancy fines, and the rise of plots centred on Mary — Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington all flow from this moment.

Why the Revolt Mattered

In February 1570 Pope Pius V issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Elizabeth and absolving English Catholics of their loyalty to her. From this moment, Catholicism and treason were officially linked in Elizabethan minds. Parliament responded in 1571 with the Treasons Act, making it a capital offence to deny Elizabeth’s right to rule, and tightened recusancy fines on Catholics who skipped Anglican services. Mary, already a magnet for Catholic hopes, became the unavoidable centre of every later plot. And the old independent power of the northern nobility — the medieval ‘over-mighty subjects’ who had threatened earlier monarchs — was effectively broken.

A lower-band answer says the revolt ‘showed Elizabeth was vulnerable’. A top-band answer connects it forward: the failure of an open military rebellion pushed Catholic resistance underground, which is why every later threat — Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586 — took the form of a secret plot, requiring Walsingham’s spy network to expose. The revolt didn’t just fail; it changed the type of threat Elizabeth faced for the next eighteen years.

By the spring of 1570 Elizabeth was, on paper, more secure: the rebels were dead or in exile, the north was loyal, and the nobility had been reminded that defying the Crown ended badly. Yet the Pope had just declared open season on her, the Privy Council under William Cecil and Francis Walsingham was now permanently on alert, and the long shadow of Mary, Queen of Scots stretched ahead for another seventeen years. The Northern Rebellion failed in the field, but it set the agenda for everything that followed.
